steps.text: Fill a large pot halfway full with water and bring to a boil. Adjust heat so water just simmers.
Meanwhile, mix together flour, nutmeg, salt, and white pepper in a medium bowl.
Whisk eggs together in a small bowl.
Add eggs alternately with milk to dry ingredients. Stir until smooth.
Working in batches, press dough through a spaetzle maker, or through a large-holed colander or metal grater, into simmering water.
Cook 5 to 8 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon or spider and drain well.
Melt butter in a large skillet. Add spaetzle and cook, stirring gently, until heated through.

raw_recipe.headline: German Spaetzle Dumplings
raw_recipe.description: A side of spaetzle is pure comfort. These noodle-like German dumplings are easy to mix up, then boiled in water and given a quick sauté in butter. Yum!

video.description: These traditional German dumplings are boiled then fried in butter.

review.reviewBody: Great recipe, the flavor is BETTER! than our favorite authentic German restaurant. The nutmeg makes it so good, my family raved. I served this with pot roast in a red wine, mushroom gravy and roasted asparagus. Thanks for sharing this recipe!! **By the way, a Ziptop bag with 4 or 5 small wholes punched with a skewer was a lot easier to handle than the strainer method. The texture was more authentic as well.

These are wonderful. My kids love them. I do not have a Spaetzle maker, so i use a flat cheese grater. The first few times I made these I burned my hand a few times. *** Last time I used two clothespins to secure the grater to the edge of my pot. It worked perfectly!*** No more burns and the preparation went so much quicker.

This is my second time attempting to leave a review - the site decided to delete my first one when I hit the "made it" button, and wouldn't allow me to leave the dialog box without adding a rating, which was blank and overwrote my first submission - not a very smartly designed website.

I referenced Cooking MaMa's review prior to making and found, as she did, that the recipe as stated leaves you with a dough that isn't quite right - it was too sticky to properly work; thus, the rating. However I was able to remedy the problem on the fly by dusting the dough with a little extra flour a few times. I believe I ended up using about an extra quarter cup, give or take.

I decided to go more traditional and press the dough out to about 1/4" with my hand and then cut ~1//4" strips with a dough knife, which I then cut by eye resulting in pre-cooked pieces of about a cube shape to about a one inch strip. This method results in less uniform noodles with little pits and grooves that hold sauce well - one of the things I really like about this type of noodle. 

I tossed about 15-20 pieces at a time into well-salted rolling water and spidered them out once they floated to the top (about a minute or so), and into a colander to drain and cool. The resulting noodle was just al dente', which should be about perfect when I cook them later this evening in herbed (sage, thyme, tarragon) brown butter with porcini.

Pretty good. I make pasta and potato dumplings so I have experience with this type of dough and recipe. First, use less milk about half what is called for. It will make for easier handling. I would use a little less nutmeg - personal preference but maybe 1/4+ tsp would give a nice hint of flavor. I took advice to use pastry bag piping 2 inch pieces into salted boiling water - it worked well. I tried the strainer - complete mess. Zip lock bag would work if you don't have pastry supplies.
Texture was perfect - be careful not to over cook. This is a keeper with a little tweaking.

Bought a spaetlzle-maker just for this. I added prosciutto, chopped jalapenos, and shredded parmesan cheese to this when serving as a main course. This was based on a dish called 'teufelsnockerl' (beware the false hits about a music group!) that I had in Vienna some years ago (restaurant is gone, wasn't able to find it. It was in Favoriten near Rainers Hotel in 2017 if anyone cares). I also prepared it as in the recipe as a side for pork schnitzel, which was about the size of a dinner plate at that restaurant, and somewhat smaller when I made it.

Thank you StickySue for your wonderful advice today on the Buzz. Because I didn’t have a spaetzle maker, StickySue recommended I take a plastic bag and punch 6 to 8 holes in it with a clean knitting needle or pen; spray the inside of the bag very lightly; put the dough into the bag and squeeze into the boiling water slowly. They came out perfect! We thought they made an excellent side dish.

I just made these. My first time making spaetzle. I was scared, but it was a success!! The only thing I did different was double the recipe and use half the amount of nutmeg because it’s such a potent spice. It was perfect and I don’t recommend leaving it out. I let the “dough” rest for 30 minutes before using my flat cheese grater as the tool. I also watched a couple YouTube videos just to see what the consistency should be since I’ve never made it before and this recipe was spot on. I made to go with chicken paprikash. It was so easy and they are so delicious I will find other uses for this recipe soon!!!

Tastes just like Oma used to make! Don't leave out the nutmeg - it gives an authentic taste. My favourite accompaniment is portobello mushrooms sautéed in butter with garlic and onion. Add a little flour, stir to combine then add some vegetable stock to make a gravy. Lecker Schmecker!!

This recipe makes wonderful authentic German spaetzle. I generally double or triple the recipe to make enough for freezing. I use a potato mincer to make the dumpling, and freeze them in meal-sized portions before sautéing them. I sauté them when I thaw them for use. I also add a couple of minced garlic cloves to the recipe because we like the garlic flavor. 

These dumplings freeze well, and I find it easier to make them in large batches and freeze them to have them handy when I need them. I also have found that it is good to stir them as soon as you have a batch in the water. Otherwise, they fall to the bottom of the pot and stick together. A quick stir breaks them up and they don't stick together.

I use 3 eggs to a cup of flour and milk in order to gave a higher protein content. I cook them, then dehydrate in my dehydrator, and can store indefinitely in a jar. I use a Norpro spaetzle maker I got from Amazon, and it is the the perfect tool. For $10, don't skimp on bad equipment.

An easy way to do instead of a grater or strainer is to use a disposable pastry bag or zip loc bag with a small tip cut off and squeeze them into the water. I have a spaetzle maker but this is just so easy and no mess to clean up.
This is the only spaetzle recipe I have used for years. I follow it exactly as written, and it has never failed me! I love the little touch of extra flavor the nutmeg adds.
Its good with Bacon bits in it, Garlic also, just tweek to your own liking.Had some in Germany with Butter, garlic, and parcley.

This is a great spaetzle recipe - tastes much like the one at our favorite German restaurant. Love the hint of nutmeg in these. Though I'm not much of a salty person, I did find these needed a bit more salt. But that was just a personal preference. I'll be using this recipe for now on. Thanks for sharing!

I have tried many recipes and this one mirrors the one I was given when i lived and worked in Germany. When I couldn't find that recipe I tried this one and absolutely loved the way the spaetzletastes. Of course I finally found my other recipe but still use this one most of the time.
Excellent! Wouldn't change a thing! Very flavorful!

Added dehydrated onion (fresh can be used), nutmeg. Sour cream after pan browning, right before serving. Butter was used, next time I will use bacon dripping to brown. I served as side with pork cutlets (schnitzel) with a wedge of lemon. Fantastic!
Season the flower well and butter well in sauté pan.

To start with, both my husband and I are German. He came from Germany in the 1950's where as my grandparents came here in the 1900's. We do not use a spaetzle maker or collander with holes. We drop them into the water with a spoon. They look the same as your pictures. They are just "small thin dumplings" that's the difference. We love them!!!

I’ve been making Spaetzle for over 50 years and this recipe is a new favorite with our family. Two new innovations to our original recipe are: 1. Adding nutmeg to the dough, and 2. Using the stockpot’s insert to form the Spaetzle is very creative. Kudos for teaching an old hen new tricks! Thank you!!
